arXiv:0912.1388v1 [math.AP] 08 Dec 2009

Local existence and WKB approximation of solutions to Schrödinger-Poisson system in the two-dimensional whole space

Satoshi Masaki Address: Division of Mathematics
Graduate School of Information Sciences
Tohoku University
Sendai 980-8579, Japan Email address: masaki@ims.is.tohoku.ac.jp
Abstract.

We consider the Schrödinger-Poisson system in the two-dimensional whole space. A new formula of solutions to the Poisson equation is used. Although the potential term solving the Poisson equation may grow at the spatial infinity, we show the unique existence of a time-local solution for data in the Sobolev spaces by an analysis of a quantum hydrodynamical system via a modified Madelung transform. This method has been used to justify the WKB approximation of solutions to several classes of nonlinear Schrödinger equation in the semiclassical limit.

1. Introduction

In this article, we study the following Schrödinger-Poisson system

(SP) {i∂tu+12Δu=λPu,(t,x)∈ℝ1+2,−Δ​P=|u|2,∇P∈L∞,∇P→0 as |x|→∞,P(0)=0,u​(0,x)=u0​(x)\left\{\begin{aligned} &i{\partial}_{t}u+\frac{1}{2}\Delta u=\lambda Pu,\quad(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{1+2},\\ &-\Delta P=|u|^{2},\\ &\nabla P\in L^{\infty},\quad\nabla P\to 0\text{ as }|x|\to\infty,\quad P(0)=0,\\ &u(0,x)=u_{0}(x)\end{aligned}\right.

or its semiclassical version

(SPε\text{SP}^{\varepsilon}) {iε∂tuε+ε22Δuε=λPεuε,(t,x)∈ℝ1+2,−Δ​Pε=|uε|2,∇Pε∈L∞,∇Pε→0 as |x|→∞,Pε(0)=0,uε​(0,x)=u0ε​(x),\left\{\begin{aligned} &i\varepsilon{\partial}_{t}u^{\varepsilon}+\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{2}\Delta u^{\varepsilon}=\lambda P^{\varepsilon}u^{\varepsilon},\quad(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{1+2},\\ &-\Delta P^{\varepsilon}=|u^{\varepsilon}|^{2},\\ &\nabla P^{\varepsilon}\in L^{\infty},\quad\nabla P^{\varepsilon}\to 0\text{ as }|x|\to\infty,\quad P^{\varepsilon}(0)=0,\\ &u^{\varepsilon}(0,x)=u_{0}^{\varepsilon}(x),\end{aligned}\right.

where ε\varepsilon is a positive parameter corresponding to the Planck constant and λ∈ℝ∖{0}\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\} is a given physical constant. In this article, we assume that the initial data u0u_{0} and u0εu_{0}^{\varepsilon} belong to the Soblev space Hs​(ℝ2)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) with s>2s>2, and show that (SP) and ( SP ε ) have a unique time local solution in C⁡((−T,T),Hs​(ℝ2))C((-T,T);H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2})) and that, for the solution uεu^{\varepsilon} of ( SP ε ), the following WKB type approximation is valid in certain topology:

(1.1) uε​(t,x)=ei​ϕ⁡(t,x)ε​(a0+ε​a1+⋯+εN​aN+o⁡(εN)).u^{\varepsilon}(t,x)=e^{i\frac{\phi(t,x)}{\varepsilon}}(a_{0}+\varepsilon a_{1}+\cdots+\varepsilon^{N}a_{N}+o(\varepsilon^{N})).

The Schrödinger-Poisson system is one of the typical example of a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a nonlocal nonlinearity, and there are much literature on this system if space dimension is larger than or equal to three (see [8] and references therein).

However, in contrast with higher dimensional cases, the two-dimensional case is less studied. One of the reason may be that an appropriate meaning of a solution to the Poisson equation is not so clear. We briefly recall the treatment of the solution in previous results. For a given function b⁡(x)⩾0b(x)\geqslant 0 on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, called background, let us replace the Poisson equation in (SP) with

(1.2) −Δ​P=|u|2−b.-\Delta P=|u|^{2}-b.

One of the most natural solution may be

P1:=ℱ−1​[1|ξ|2​ℱ​(|u|2−b)],P_{1}:=\mathcal{F}^{-1}\left[\frac{1}{|\xi|^{2}}\mathcal{F}(|u|^{2}-b)\right],

where ℱ\mathcal{F} denotes the Fourier transform. To admit this solution, the following “neutrality condition” plays a very important role:

(1.3) 2​π​ℱ​(|u⁡(t)|2−b)​(0)=∫ℝ2(|u⁡(x,t)|2−b⁡(x))​𝑑x≡0.2\pi\mathcal{F}(|u(t)|^{2}-b)(0)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(|u(x,t)|^{2}-b(x))dx\equiv 0.

To handle the strong singularity of |ξ|−2​ℱ​(|u|2−b)|\xi|^{-2}\mathcal{F}(|u|^{2}-b) at the origin, this mean-zero assumption is almost essential. Indeed, in [4, 14, 21], (1.3) and several integrability conditions on ℱ⁡(|u|2−b)\mathcal{F}(|u|^{2}-b) are assumed to prove that P1P_{1} belongs to some Lebesgue space.

One of the main point in this article is to remove the neutrality condition. To make this point clear, we restrict our attention to the zero-background case b≡0b\equiv 0 throughout this article. Notice that all nontrivial solutions are excluded when we assume the neutrality condition with b≡0b\equiv 0, and so that the zero-background case is out of the framework of the previous results. In this article, the Poisson equation −Δ​P=|u|2-\Delta P=|u|^{2} is posed with the following conditions:

∇P∈L∞,∇P→0 as |x|→∞,andP(0)=0.\nabla P\in L^{\infty},\quad\nabla P\to 0\text{ as }|x|\to\infty,\quad\text{and}\quad P(0)=0.

Under these conditions, the solution PP is given by

(1.4) P(x)=−12​π∫ℝ2(log|x−y||y|)|u(y)|2dyP(x)=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(\log\frac{|x-y|}{|y|}\right)|u(y)|^{2}dy

and unique for a class of |u|2|u|^{2} (see Theorem A.1). It might seem to be more natural to use the Newtonian potential

P2​(x):=−12​π​(log⁡|x|∗|u|2)​(x),P_{2}(x):=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\left(\log|x|*|u|^{2}\right)(x),

as the solution of the Poisson equation. However, PP given in (1.4) makes sense merely if |u|2∈Lp​(ℝ2)|u|^{2}\in L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) for some p∈(1,2)p\in(1,2), and P2P_{2} requires an additional assumption ∫ℝ2(log⁡|y|)​|u⁡(y)|2​𝑑y<∞\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(\log|y|)|u(y)|^{2}dy<\infty to make sense (see Proposition A.4). Namely, PP is well-defined under a weaker assumption. This is the reason why we consider (1.4). It will turn out that the behavior of PP at the spatial infinity is not so good; in general, |P⁡(x)|=O⁡(‖u‖L22​log⁡|x|)|P(x)|=O(\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{L^{2}}^{2}\log|x|) as |x|→∞|x|\to\infty. It is worth mentioning that ∇P\nabla P never belongs to L2​(ℝ2)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) for all u≢0u\not\equiv 0 no matter how fast uu decays, say even if u∈C0∞​(ℝ2)u\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}). We discuss the Poisson equation in the two-dimensional whole space more precisely in Appendix A.

In what follows, we consider (1.4) as the solution of the Poisson equation. With (1.4), the system (SP) and ( SP ε ) are rewritten as

(SP′\text{SP}^{\prime}) {i​∂tu+12​Δ​u=λ​P​u,P=−12​π∫ℝ2(log|x−y||y|)|u(y)|2dy,u​(0,x)=u0​(x)\left\{\begin{aligned} &i{\partial}_{t}u+\frac{1}{2}\Delta u=\lambda Pu,\\ &P=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(\log\frac{|x-y|}{|y|}\right)|u(y)|^{2}dy,\\ &u(0,x)=u_{0}(x)\end{aligned}\right.

and

(SPε′\text{SP}^{\varepsilon\prime}) {i​ε​∂tuε+ε22​Δ​uε=λ​Pε​uε,Pε=−12​π∫ℝ2(log|x−y||y|)|uε(y)|2dy,uε​(0,x)=u0ε​(x),\left\{\begin{aligned} &i\varepsilon{\partial}_{t}u^{\varepsilon}+\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{2}\Delta u^{\varepsilon}=\lambda P^{\varepsilon}u^{\varepsilon},\\ &P^{\varepsilon}=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(\log\frac{|x-y|}{|y|}\right)|u^{\varepsilon}(y)|^{2}dy,\\ &u^{\varepsilon}(0,x)=u_{0}^{\varepsilon}(x),\end{aligned}\right.

respectively. The difficulty for solving ( SP ′ ) (and ( SP ε ′ )) lies in the growth |P⁡(x)|=O⁡(log⁡|x|)|P(x)|=O(\log|x|) at the spatial infinity. For example, the Duhamel term of the corresponding integral equation does not necessarily belong to any Lebesgue space because of this growth, and so we cannot apply directly the usual perturbation argument to the integral equation.

Thus, we apply another method: We look for the solution of the form

(1.5) uε​(t,x)=aε​(t,x)​ei​ϕε​(t,x)ε,u^{\varepsilon}(t,x)=a^{\varepsilon}(t,x)e^{i\frac{\phi^{\varepsilon}(t,x)}{\varepsilon}},

where the “amplitude part” aεa^{\varepsilon} is complex-valued and the “phase part” ϕε\phi^{\varepsilon} is real-valued. We are considering only ( SP ε ′ ) because ( SP ′ ) corresponds to the special case ε=1\varepsilon=1. Plugging (1.5) to ( SP ε ′ ), we obtain the following system according to the order of ε\varepsilon:

(1.6) {∂taε+∇ϕε⋅∇aε+12​aε​Δ​ϕε=i​ε2​Δ​aε,∂tϕε+12​|∇ϕε|2+λ​Pε=0,Pε(t,x)=−12​π∫ℝ2(log|x−y||y|)|aε(t,y)|2dy,aε​(0,x)=Aε​(x),ϕε​(0,x)=Φ⁡(x)\left\{\begin{aligned} &{\partial}_{t}a^{\varepsilon}+\nabla\phi^{\varepsilon}\cdot\nabla a^{\varepsilon}+\frac{1}{2}a^{\varepsilon}\Delta\phi^{\varepsilon}=i\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\Delta a^{\varepsilon},\\ &{\partial}_{t}\phi^{\varepsilon}+\frac{1}{2}|\nabla\phi^{\varepsilon}|^{2}+\lambda P^{\varepsilon}=0,\\ &P^{\varepsilon}(t,x)=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(\log\frac{|x-y|}{|y|}\right)|a^{\varepsilon}(t,y)|^{2}dy,\\ &a^{\varepsilon}(0,x)=A^{\varepsilon}(x),\quad\phi^{\varepsilon}(0,x)=\Phi(x)\end{aligned}\right.

with u0ε=Aε​ei​Φ/εu^{\varepsilon}_{0}=A^{\varepsilon}e^{i\Phi/\varepsilon}. Notice that if (aε,ϕε)(a^{\varepsilon},\phi^{\varepsilon}) solves (1.6), then uε=aε​ei​ϕε/εu^{\varepsilon}=a^{\varepsilon}e^{i\phi^{\varepsilon}/\varepsilon} is an exact solution of ( SP ε ′ ). This decomposition, called a modified Madelung transform, is first introduced in [13] to justify the WKB approximation (1.1) of solutions to a class of nonlinear Schrödinger equations, and extended to several types of nonlinear Schrödinger equations in [2, 3, 16] (see also [6, 9, 11, 12]). For the WKB approximation of the Schrödinger-Poisson system for other dimensions, we refer the reader to [17] (one dimension) and [1, 7, 18] (three dimensions and higher). In [14, 21], the same limit is treated in the two-dimensional case by Wigner measures.

Before stating our result precisely, we make some definitions and notation. Lp​(ℝ2)L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) (p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty]) and Hs​(ℝ2)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) (s⩾0s\geqslant 0) denote the usual Lebesgue and Sobolev space, respectively. We say f∈Hlocs​(ℝ2)f\in H^{s}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) if any restriction of ff on a bounded domain belongs to Hs​(ℝ2)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}). Xs​(ℝ2)X^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) is the Zhidkov space defined by

Xs​(ℝ2):={f∈L∞​(ℝ2);∇f∈Hs−1​(ℝ2)},\displaystyle X^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}):=\{f\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2});\nabla f\in H^{s-1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\},
‖f‖Xs​(ℝ2):=‖f‖L∞​(ℝ2)+‖∇f‖Hs−1​(ℝ2)\displaystyle\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{X^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}:=\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}+\left\lVert\nabla f\right\rVert_{H^{s-1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}

for s>1s>1. This space is introduced in [22] (see also [10]). We sometimes write Lp=Lp​(ℝ2)L^{p}=L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), Hs=Hs​(ℝ2)H^{s}=H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), and Xs=Xs​(ℝ2)X^{s}=X^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), for short.

1.1. Main result 1

We first state our result on the unique existence of a local solution to ( SP ′ ).

Theorem 1.1.

Let u0∈Hs​(ℝ2)u_{0}\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) with s>2s>2. Then, there exist an existence time T=T⁡(‖u0‖Hs−1​(ℝ2))T=T(\left\lVert u_{0}\right\rVert_{H^{s-1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}) and a time-local solution u∈C⁡((−T,T),Hs​(ℝ2))∩C1​((−T,T),Hlocs−2​(ℝ2))u\in C((-T,T);H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))\cap C^{1}((-T,T);H^{s-2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})) to ( SP ′ ). Moreover, this solution is unique in this space and the data-to-solution mapping u0↦uu_{0}\mapsto u is continuous from Hs​(ℝ2)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) to C⁡((−T,T),Hs−1​(ℝ2))C((-T,T);H^{s-1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})). Furthermore, the mass is conserved.

Remark 1.2.

The existence part of Theorem 1.1 holds if u0∈Hs​(ℝ2)u_{0}\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) (s>1s>1).

Remark 1.3.

For the solution uu given in Theorem 1.1, ∂tu{\partial}_{t}u does not necessarily decays at the spatial infinity. This is due to the lack of spatial decay of PP. Therefore, in general, u∈C1​((−T,T),Hlocs−2​(ℝ2))u\in C^{1}((-T,T);H^{s-2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})) is not replaced by u∈C1​((−T,T),Hs−2​(ℝ2))u\in C^{1}((-T,T);H^{s-2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})). Nevertheless, the solution is continuous as a Hs​(ℝ2)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2})-valued function.

Remark 1.4.

The uniqueness of the solution is new in the sense not only that the result itself is new but also that we use a new argument. In our proof, we derive the uniqueness of ( SP ′ ) from that of the system (1.6) via (1.5) by showing that every solution of ( SP ′ ) is of the form (1.5), at least for small time.

Remark 1.5.

The solution given by Theorem 1.1 does not necessarily have a finite energy. The energy

E⁡[u]​(t)=12​‖∇u​(t)‖L22−λ4​π​∬ℝ2×ℝ2(log⁡|x−y|)​|u⁡(t,x)|2​|u⁡(t,y)|2​𝑑x​𝑑yE[u](t)=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\nabla u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{2}}^{2}-\frac{\lambda}{4\pi}\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2}\times\mathbb{R}^{2}}(\log|x-y|)|u(t,x)|^{2}|u(t,y)|^{2}dxdy

is finite and conserved as long as W⁡(t):=∫0t∫ℝ2(log⁡|y|)​|u⁡(s,y)|2​𝑑y​𝑑sW(t):=\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(\log|y|)|u(s,y)|^{2}dyds is finite. Indeed, if W⁡(t)<∞W(t)<\infty then u~​(t)=u⁡(t)​ei​λ2​π​W​(t)\widetilde{u}(t)=u(t)e^{i\frac{\lambda}{2\pi}W(t)} solves

(1.7) i∂tu~+12Δu~=−λ2​πu~∫ℝ2(log|x−y|)|u~(y)|2dyi{\partial}_{t}\widetilde{u}+\frac{1}{2}\Delta\widetilde{u}=-\frac{\lambda}{2\pi}\widetilde{u}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(\log|x-y|)|\widetilde{u}(y)|^{2}dy

and E​[u~]​(t)E[\widetilde{u}](t) is conserved. Then, one sees that E⁡[u]=E⁡[u~]E[{u}]=E[\widetilde{u}] is also conserved. The ground state for (1.7) is studied in [19].

Theorem 1.7.

Let Assumption 1.6 be satisfied for a positive integer NN. Our analysis is still valid in the presence of background. The rest of this article is organized as follows: In Section 2, we first show the existence of a solution to the system (1.6) on which our main theorems are all based. Then, we prove Theorems 1.1 and 1.7 in Sections 3 and 4, respectively. In Appendix A, we summarize results on the Poisson equation in the two-dimensional whole space. They play important roles in our argument.

2. Preliminary result

In this section, we establish an existence result on the system

3.3. Uniqueness

To complete the proof of Theorem 1.1, we show that the solution uu is unique. It is important to note that the uniqueness of the system (3.1) does not directly means that of ( SP ′ ). Namely, it implies no more than that the solution of ( SP ′ ) which is written as u=a​ei​ϕu=ae^{i\phi} with a solution (a,ϕ)(a,\phi) of (3.1), is unique. Then, what to show is that all solution of ( SP ′ ) is written as u=a​ei​ϕu=ae^{i\phi} with a solution (a,ϕ)(a,\phi) of (3.1).

Lemma 3.5.

Let s>2s>2 and define

A:=C⁡([0,T),Hs​(ℝ2))∩C1​((0,T),Hlocs−2​(ℝ2))\displaystyle A:=C([0,T);H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))\cap C^{1}((0,T);H^{s-2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))
B:={ϕ∈C1​([0,T)×ℝ2);∇ϕ∈Xs+1​(ℝ2)∩L2+​(ℝ2)}.\displaystyle B:=\left\{\phi\in C^{1}([0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^{2});\nabla\phi\in X^{s+1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\cap L^{2+}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\right\}.

At first, we define mappings ff and gg by

f:\displaystyle f:{} A×B∋(a,ϕ)↦(a​ei​ϕ,ϕ),\displaystyle A\times B\ni(a,\phi)\mapsto(ae^{i\phi},\phi),
g:\displaystyle g:{} A×B∋(u,ψ)↦(u​e−i​ψ,ψ).\displaystyle A\times B\ni(u,\psi)\mapsto(ue^{-i\psi},\psi).

By means of (3.2), we see that the images of ff and gg are both subspaces of A×BA\times B. It is easy to verify that ff and gg are injective, and that f∘g=g∘f=Idf\circ g=g\circ f=\mathrm{Id}. Therefore, both ff and gg are bijection from A×BA\times B to itself and f−1=gf^{-1}=g.

Assume that (a,ϕ)∈A×B(a,\phi)\in A\times B is a unique solution of (3.1). Then, (u,ψ)=f⁡(a,ϕ)(u,\psi)=f(a,\phi) solves (3.5), and this solution is unique since ff is bijective. In the same way, if (u,ψ)(u,\psi) is a unique solution of (3.5), then (a,ϕ)=f−1​(u,ψ)(a,\phi)=f^{-1}(u,\psi) is a unique solution of (3.1). ∎

Remark 3.6.

In Lemma 3.5, the gauge invariance of the nonlinearity P​uPu, that is, the property that PP depends only on the modulus |u||u| and is independent of the argument u/|u|u/|u|, is fully employed. By this property, it turns out that solutions of two Hamilton-Jacobi equations in (3.1) and in (3.5) are identical.

Remark 4.5.

The feature of the two-dimensional case is that not only ϕ0\phi_{0} but also all of ϕj\phi_{j} (j⩾1j\geqslant 1) may grow at the spatial infinity though they are identically zero at the initial time. This growth comes from Poisson terms (see (A.11)). This is why amplitudes are required to be in some weighted L2L^{2} space.

Appendix A Poisson equation in the two dimensional whole space

In this appendix, we consider the Poisson equation

(A.1) −Δ​P=fin ​ℝ2-\Delta P=f\quad\text{in }\mathbb{R}^{2}

with the conditions

(A.2) |∇P|→0​ as ​|x|→∞,P⁡(0)=0,\displaystyle|\nabla P|\to 0\text{ as }|x|\to\infty,\quad P(0)=0,
(A.3) ∇P∈L∞​(ℝ2).\displaystyle\nabla P\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}).

We briefly recall the higher dimension case n⩾3n\geqslant 3. It is well known that the solution PP is defined by the Fourier transform or by the Newtonian potential as

(A.4) P⁡(x)=\displaystyle P(x)={} ℱ−1​[1|ξ|2​ℱ​f​(ξ)]​(x)\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{-1}\left[\frac{1}{|\xi|^{2}}\mathcal{F}f(\xi)\right](x)
(A.5) =\displaystyle={} 1n⁡(n−2)​ωn​(|x|2−n∗f)​(x),\displaystyle\frac{1}{n(n-2)\omega_{n}}(|x|^{2-n}*f)(x),

where ωn\omega_{n} denotes the volume of the unit sphere in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. In this case, it can be said that (A.1) in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} is posed with the condition

(A.6) P→0​ as ​|x|→∞,P∈L∞​(ℝn).P\to 0\text{ as }|x|\to\infty,\quad P\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}).

For a good ff, say f∈𝒮⁡(ℝn)f\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), the solution PP defined by (A.4) or (A.5) satisfies (A.6), and is unique by Liouville’s theorem.

In the two dimensional case, it is not possible to define the solution by (A.4) in general (even in the distribution sense) because of the singularity of |ξ|−2|\xi|^{-2}. In [4, 21, 14], the definition (A.4) is employed under several assumption on ff which provides ℱ​f​(ξ)=O⁡(|ξ|)\mathcal{F}f(\xi)=O(|\xi|) as ξ→0\xi\to 0. To realize it, it is almost necessary to suppose the following neutrality condition:

(A.7) 2​π​ℱ​f​(0)=∫ℝ2f⁡(x)​𝑑x=0.2\pi\mathcal{F}f(0)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}f(x)dx=0.

This condition is, however, very restrictive in some case. For example, in our systems (SP) or ( SP ε ), this condition excludes all nontrivial solutions. To avoid such a situation, we observe the fact that

(A.8) ℱ−1​[−i​ξ|ξ|2​ℱ​f​(ξ)]​(x)\mathcal{F}^{-1}\left[\frac{-i\xi}{|\xi|^{2}}\mathcal{F}f(\xi)\right](x)

(which may be equal to ∇P\nabla P) is well-defined even in the two-dimensional case, and we modify the condition (A.6) into (A.2)–(A.3), so that the Poisson equation (A.1) has a solution. The idea is the following: If the gradient of PP was defined uniquely, then PP should be given uniquely by the line integral of it under P⁡(0)=0P(0)=0.

A.1. A solution given by the Newtonian potential

We can also give a rigorous meaning of the Newtonian potential

(A.14) P~(x)=−12​π∫ℝ2(log|x−y|)f(y)dy\widetilde{P}(x)=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(\log|x-y|)f(y)dy

as a solution of the Poisson equation. Notice that −12​π​log⁡|x|-\frac{1}{2\pi}\log|x| is the Newtonian kernel in two dimensions and so that P~\widetilde{P} is a two-dimensional version of (A.5).

Proposition A.4.

Let f∈Lp0​(ℝ2)f\in L^{p_{0}}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) for some p0∈(1,2)p_{0}\in(1,2) and let P~\widetilde{P} be as in (A.14). If P~​(x)\widetilde{P}(x) is finite at some x∈ℝ2x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, then it is finite for all x∈ℝ2x\in\mathbb{R}^{2} and, moreover, P~​(x)=P​(x)+P~​(0)\widetilde{P}(x)=P(x)+\widetilde{P}(0), where PP is the solution of (A.1) with (A.2)–(A.3) given by Theorem A.1.

Notice that the proposition implies the following:

  • •

    If P~​(x)\widetilde{P}(x) diverges at some x∈ℝ2x\in\mathbb{R}^{2} then it necessarily diverges for all x∈ℝ2x\in\mathbb{R}^{2} under the same assumption on ff.

  • •

    The difference between PP and P~\widetilde{P} is merely a constant P~​(0)\widetilde{P}(0). However, when we consider P~\widetilde{P}, we need an additional assumption on ff only for saying that this constant is finite.

  • •

    If f∈Lp0​(ℝ2)f\in L^{p_{0}}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) is so that P~​(0)\widetilde{P}(0) is finite, then P~\widetilde{P} is a weak solution of (A.1) with the condition P​(0)=P~​(0)P(0)=\widetilde{P}(0) and |∇P|→0|\nabla P|\to 0 as |x|→∞|x|\to\infty.

The proof of this proposition is obvious: It suffices to mention that, for any f∈Lp0​(ℝ2)f\in L^{p_{0}}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) (p0∈(1,2)p_{0}\in(1,2)) and x1x_{1}, x2∈ℝ2x_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{2},

−12​π∫ℝ2(log|x1−y||x2−y|)f(y)dy-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(\log\frac{|x_{1}-y|}{|x_{2}-y|}\right)f(y)dy
